knownGaps: Cancellation has no dedicated event. A user interrupt surfaces as session.error carrying error.name=MessageAbortedError, immediately followed by session.status{idle} and session.idle. An adapter that ignores the error name cannot tell a cancelled turn from a failed one: a provider auth failure emits the identical event shape with error.name=ProviderAuthError. The lane is correct either way because session.status is state-shaped; only the terminal outcome depends on reading the name.
Subagent activity has no dedicated event. Child sessions are identifiable only by info.parentID on session events.

The blocked lane is transition-shaped, not state-shaped: session.status only ever carried busy or idle, and blocking is visible solely as the permission.asked/permission.replied pair. A dropped permission.asked therefore does not self-correct the way a dropped busy/idle does.

tool.execute.after did not fire on 1.18.23 even though tool.execute.before did, so tool completion cannot be relied on as an event. The cancellation traces used a tool-free prompt and did not re-test this on 1.18.25.

Both ~/.config/opencode/plugin/ and ~/.config/opencode/plugins/ are loaded, and an asset present in both fires every event twice. The installer must own exactly one path and repair must detect the other.

Every export of a plugin module must be a plugin factory. One non-function export and the module is imported and then never called, silently and with no error. Measured on 1.18.25 with four probe plugins. This is invisible to offline tests: the plugin installs cleanly, its unit tests pass, and it reports nothing at all.

There is no event ordering guarantee across separate report processes. Reports must be serialized by the integration, because the lifecycle store enforces a strictly increasing sequence per run and correctly rejects an out-of-order arrival.
sourceVersionNote: Traced against opencode 1.18.23 (Phase A) and 1.18.25 (Phase B cancellation) on darwin/arm64, 2026-08-30. Docs page states no version or stability level; the hook interface was cross-read from packages/plugin/src/index.ts.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single SessionStart hook: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects. Codex's own contract is far broader and is now fully traced (see the next gap), so the ceiling here is what Sidecar ships rather than what Codex can do.

Codex's full lifecycle IS traced and would support the full tier once an adapter ships for it. Real captures on 0.151.0 cover work start (UserPromptSubmit), tool use (PreToolUse/PostToolUse), blocking (PermissionRequest, the last event before the pane blocks), unblocking (PostToolUse on approval), turn completion (Stop), cancellation (Interrupt, captured by two independent routes), session identity (SessionStart) and process exit (SessionEnd). Every event carries session_id and, from UserPromptSubmit onward, turn_id.

Four of the twelve events the shipped binary enumerates were NOT traced: SubagentStart, SubagentStop, PreCompact and PostCompact. The handoff says the evidence supports the full tier, and it does for every transition the promotion gate names — but the gate also names compaction and sub-agent isolation, and those rest on the binary's embedded schemas rather than on a capture. So it is unknown whether a sub-agent's events carry a distinguishing field the way Claude's agent_id does; if they do not, a sub-agent's tool calls are indistinguishable from the pane conversation's and would drive the pane's lane. opencode and pi both carry a sub-agent gap for the same reason, and Codex's silence about one was an omission rather than a clean bill of health.

Denying a permission request emits Interrupt, not PostToolUse and not Stop. Interrupt is therefore the universal 'the turn ended without completing' signal and the blocked lane always resolves; an adapter that treats only PostToolUse as the unblock would latch on blocked whenever a user says no.
SessionEnd does not fire under `codex exec` at all. It was observed only in the interactive TUI, so process exit on a non-interactive run is detectable only by process liveness.

No event re-asserts state. Unlike OpenCode's session.status, every Codex event is transition-shaped, so a dropped or missed event does not self-correct and an adapter cannot rely on the next event to repair the lane.

The trusted_hash is computed over the EFFECTIVE hook, after Codex clamps it, not over the hook as written. Codex clamps SessionEnd and Interrupt hook timeouts to 3s and prints a warning naming hooks.json on every start. A pre-written record for those two events at Sidecar's canonical timeout of 10 does not match, and the user gets the interactive 'Hooks need review' prompt. Proved by letting Codex write its own records and diffing them: the identity hashed with timeout=3 matches byte-for-byte and timeout=10 does not. Any lifecycle adapter must declare timeout<=3 on those two events.

Hooks are disabled by default behind features.hooks, so the integration must edit config.toml as well as hooks.json: three owned mutations (entry, feature flag, trust record) rather than one. Uninstall deliberately leaves features.hooks on, because other installed hooks may depend on it.

Codex only auto-runs hooks whose trusted_hash in config.toml matches a hash of the hook's normalized identity; an untrusted hook triggers an interactive 'Hooks need review' prompt. Sidecar pre-writes the record using the algorithm reproduced from codex-rs; it is now live-verified across eleven distinct event names in a single run rather than the one session_start vector, which is considerably stronger evidence that the reproduction is correct. It remains a provider implementation detail rather than a published contract, and if it drifts the failure mode is that visible one-time prompt, not a silent loss.

Trust records are keyed by the hook's position in hooks.json (path:event:group:hook). Any edit that reorders groups, by the user or by Sidecar removing its own group when others follow it, silently invalidates the trust records of the hooks that shifted, and Codex re-prompts for them.

config.toml is edited by a line writer with a TOML parser as its read-only oracle. A config.toml containing a genuine multi-line string (a structural triple-quote delimiter) is refused outright: install, repair and uninstall all decline rather than guess where a table header ends, so the integration is unavailable to a user whose config uses one. A delimiter appearing inside a comment or an ordinary single-line string no longer refuses. The scanner also declines any key = value line it cannot normalise, which is stricter than necessary. All of these fail in the safe direction.
The integration manages ~/.codex only; a CODEX_HOME override relocates the provider's configuration where the installer does not look.

Herdr shipped a full-lifecycle Codex hook set through eight asset versions and then deliberately removed it, retaining SessionStart for session identity only. Sidecar's own traces do not reproduce a reason for that rollback: every transition such a hook set needs is observable on 0.151.0. It stays recorded as unexplained rather than refuted, because a contract that held in one capture session is not the same as one that holds across versions.
sourceVersionNote: codex-cli 0.151.0 on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-08-30 into an isolated CODEX_HOME with hooks that recorded event names only, on a private tmux socket; the user's real ~/.codex was never written. Traces are in testdata/traces/codex. The published config-reference URL redirects and truncates before the hooks section; the authoritative contract is codex-rs/app-server-protocol HookEventName plus the JSON schemas embedded in the shipped binary, which enumerate PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, UserPromptSubmit, Stop and Interrupt.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single SessionStart hook entry: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects.

Claude's lifecycle is traced and supports ADVISORY, not full. Real captures on 2.1.220 cover work start (UserPromptSubmit), tool use (PreToolUse/PostToolUse), blocking (PermissionRequest plus a Notification), turn completion (Stop), session identity (SessionStart) and process exit (SessionEnd). What is missing is a contract gap rather than a tracing gap; see below.

PermissionRequest DOES fire on the current release, correcting an earlier docs-only reading of this entry which held that session identity was all Claude offered. Blocking is first-class: PreToolUse, then PermissionRequest, then Notification, and then nothing at all until the user answers.

PostToolUse is silently skipped for any tool that went through the interactive permission prompt. The same tool with no prompt fires it normally. An adapter that unblocks on PostToolUse therefore unblocks on exactly the turns that never blocked, and never on the ones that did.

No user-cancellation event exists at all. Interrupting a live turn with Escape produced no hook event whatsoever: not Stop, and not any of the speculative event names Claude accepted into its settings without complaint. Denying a permission request, or Escape-cancelling the prompt, is equally silent. Because Stop does not fire either, a state machine driven only by these hooks latches on working or blocked forever. This is the single gap that caps Claude below full lifecycle authority, and no amount of further tracing can close it.
Stop means stopped generating, not ready for input, so turn completion cannot be taken from it without reconciliation against screen state.

Both halves of Herdr's stated reason for removing its own full-lifecycle Claude hook set, missed permission results and escape interrupts, are independently reproduced here on the current release. That rollback is now explained rather than merely recorded.

Hook configuration merges additively across five layers (enterprise, project, local, user, plugin), so Sidecar can own exactly its one entry in ~/.claude/settings.json and can never own the effective hook set; another layer can add, but not remove, hooks beside it.

The integration manages the settings.json under Claude's own configuration home, which is CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when that names an absolute directory and ~/.claude otherwise. That is Claude's own resolution, so a relocated Claude is found by status, install and uninstall alike. What Sidecar still cannot see is the rest of the merge: a hook another layer contributes is not in this file.

grok reads hooks from ~/.claude/settings.json by design -- its shipped documentation carries a 'Claude Code Compatibility' section for exactly that -- so Sidecar's installed Claude entry also fires inside grok sessions. That no longer binds anything: report-session resolves --kind through the catalog and then checks it against the pane's own occupant, so the Claude entry firing inside grok is refused with kind_mismatch rather than bound. Fixed and closed as td-11040b.
sourceVersionNote: claude 2.1.220 on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-08-30. Hooks were injected with the additive --settings flag and an isolated working directory, so nothing in the user's ~/.claude was written; the interactive half ran on a private tmux socket. Traces are in testdata/traces/claude. Recording captured event names and field names only, never any field value.

knownGaps: TRACED, and the tier is the ceiling the traces can reach. Four sanitized captures of pi 0.84.3 are in testdata/traces/pi: a successful turn, a turn that called a tool, a user cancellation, and a provider-error turn followed by /quit. They cover work start (agent_start), turn completion (agent_settled) and session identity (session_start with ctx.sessionFile present), which is exactly what the shipped asset reports and exactly what `covered` claims. `advisory` is the ceiling rather than a waypoint: `full` needs blocked_on_request and unblocked, and no released Pi can produce either.

The traces are what the asset's two invisible guards rest on, and they measure both. ctx.isIdle is FALSE on agent_end and TRUE on agent_settled three milliseconds later, so an asset that closed a turn on agent_end would report idle while Pi still considers the run active. And turn_start/turn_end fire TWICE inside one agent run when a tool is called -- once around the tool call, once around the reply -- so a turn in Pi's vocabulary is a provider round trip and turn_end is not turn completion either. agent_settled fires once, at the end. See traces/pi/simple-turn.tsv and traces/pi/tool-turn.tsv.

`sidecar agent start --kind pi` still times out, and the hooks lane cannot fix it. The tool turn ran a bash command with no permission event, so the pane is reachable; what refuses is the process gate. Pi installs as a `#!/usr/bin/env node` shim, tmux reports the pane's foreground command as `node`, and DetectPi returns pi.process-mismatch before any manifest rule is evaluated. The screen lane by itself answers idle for the same capture (`sidecar agent explain --file` gives state=idle, fallback_reason=default_known_agent_idle_fallback), so widening the process gate is the whole fix -- and that is the parity plan's Slice 3, not this one. No tier promotion reaches it either: agentcontrol's detector calls agentactivity.Detect only and never consults the lifecycle store.

The blocked lane is structurally unreachable, not merely untraced, so `full` can never be earned. Pi ships no permission system, so there is nothing to be blocked on. The only shape a Pi block could have is a cooperative extension-to-extension protocol on Pi's untyped event bus, which is what Herdr's asset listens for and what Sidecar's listens for on its own namespace -- and nothing publishes either channel. The string "herdr" does not appear in pi 0.84.3's shipped bundle at all; ExtensionAPI.on enumerates thirty events and not one is a permission, approval or prompt event; and Herdr's four occurrences of its own channel name are two listeners and two test drivers. The branch is kept and driven by a fixture so the ladder stays identical to upstream's, and the transition is not claimed. traces/pi/tool-turn.tsv adds the one thing a capture can add here: a bash tool runs unconditionally, with no permission, approval or prompt event anywhere between before_agent_start and agent_settled. It does NOT show anything about the untyped bus, because no column in that format observes one; the tracer listened on both channels and neither fired, but a fixture cannot tell that apart from never having subscribed, so the unreachability claim rests on the emitter-side reading above rather than on the capture.

Turn completion must come from agent_settled and never from agent_end. agent_end means "this attempt stopped" and Pi can follow it with an automatic retry or a compaction (_willRetryAfterAgentEnd, dist/core/agent-session.js:369), so an adapter that reported idle on it would announce a finished turn in the middle of one. The shipped asset does not subscribe to agent_end at all, and upstream's fixture asserts that absence directly.

process_exit is NOT claimed and the asset does not subscribe to session_shutdown. That event fires with reason quit, reload, new, resume or fork, so three of its five reasons are a session swap rather than an exit, and releasing the lane on those would hand a live pane back to screen detection mid-run. Sidecar already owns process liveness for every provider. The reason IS readable: the last row of traces/pi/error-turn-and-quit.tsv is session_shutdown carrying reason=quit, captured by typing /quit. So a future version that subscribed and released only on that reason could claim this; today it is unclaimed by choice, and this gap and `covered` move together when it changes.

tool_use is NOT claimed by choice, not by absence. tool_execution_start and tool_execution_end do fire and do carry toolName -- traces/pi/tool-turn.tsv records both around a bash call -- and the shipped asset subscribes to neither, because tool use is a refinement of work_start rather than a separate lane and every subscription is another event whose ordering has to be reasoned about.

Cancellation has no event, now measured rather than inferred. traces/pi/cancelled-turn.tsv is a turn interrupted with Escape; the pane printed "Operation aborted" and the event stream is byte-identical in shape to a completed turn -- turn_end, agent_end, agent_settled, same field names, nothing distinguishing. The listener stayed attached for 20s afterwards and nothing further arrived. agent_settled is emitted from a finally block, so the lane is still correct; only the terminal outcome is unknowable, which is why `cancelled` is not claimed.
There are no subagent events. An agent an extension spawns is a separate process, so nothing in Pi's event stream describes it and a parent's lane can never be derived from a child's.

The extension API publishes no version or stability guarantee, and Pi's changelog records breaking changes that have already shipped. An integration written against 0.84.3 has no contractual reason to keep working on 0.85 -- 0.84.4 was already offered as an update during the capture run -- which is why testedProviderRange is the single version actually driven and not a range.

Pi loads extensions from a project-local <cwd>/.pi/extensions as well as the user-level directory. Sidecar installs only into the user-level one: a per-project copy would follow a checkout into other people's clones and would report from panes Sidecar never set up.

PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR relocates Pi's whole agent directory, and OMP is a rebranded fork of the same codebase reading the same variable. With it set, Pi and OMP collapse onto one extension directory. Sidecar ships no OMP adapter yet, so nothing collides today; whichever adapter lands second has to refuse the collision the way Herdr's install_omp does.
sourceVersionNote: pi 0.84.3 on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-09-02 against openrouter z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (and, for the error turn, the retired stealth/ox-alpha). The contract was first read from the released package's own dist/core/extensions/types.d.ts (the event set, ctx.mode, ctx.isIdle, sessionManager.getSessionFile/getSessionId), dist/core/agent-session.js (the settle ordering that makes the isIdle guard correct) and dist/config.js (PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR, tilde-expanded, defaulting to ~/.pi/agent, with extensions loaded from <that>/extensions); every load-bearing claim in it is now backed by a capture. The traces were taken from a live Pi TUI in a Sidecar-managed shell on a private tmux server, with PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR, XDG_STATE_HOME and -config all under a scratch tree and SIDECAR_ISOLATED_STATE=1; the user's real ~/.pi was never written. Sidecar's own asset was installed by `sidecar agent integration install pi` rather than by hand, and the hooks lane was proved end to end: the store recorded idle(session_start), working(turn_start), idle(turn_complete) from source sidecar.pi.extension with a session reference bound by path. The event mapping is ported from Herdr's pi integration at HERDR_INTEGRATION_VERSION=8; see internal/agentintegration/portedfrom.go.

knownGaps: TRACED, and `advisory` is the ceiling this asset can reach rather than a waypoint. Four sanitized captures of kilo 7.5.9 are in testdata/traces/kilo: a successful turn, a turn that ran a bash tool, a turn that had to ask permission, and a provider-error turn. They cover work start (chat.message and session.status busy), blocking and unblocking (permission.asked and permission.replied), turn completion (session.status idle and session.idle) and session identity (session.created), which is exactly what the shipped asset reports and exactly what `covered` claims. `full` additionally needs `cancelled` and `process_exit`, and this asset can produce neither; both are unclaimed by choice and both are explained below.

The session.status field shape is the one genuine upstream bug this port fixes, and it is measured rather than reasoned. Kilo's session.status event carries an OBJECT whose `type` is the discriminator: the shipped schema is a union of {type:"idle"}, {type:"busy"}, {type:"retry",...} and {type:"offline",...}. Herdr's kilo asset at integration version 4 accepts a status only when `typeof status === "string"`, so on this release it maps none of them and falls through to re-reporting the session on every status event. Herdr's own opencode asset at version 10 reads `status?.type` and has done since before this port; the kilo variant never received the fix, in the same way the pi variant never received omp's Windows-path fix. Sidecar takes the fixed form, because session.status is the only state-shaped signal kilo has and an asset that cannot read it gives up the property that lets a dropped or misordered event self-correct.

`retry` is deliberately NOT in the status vocabulary, which is upstream's own list kept verbatim. A {type:"retry"} status therefore re-asserts the session binding rather than a lane. That is harmless: a retry happens inside a turn a busy assertion already opened, so the working lane is already correct. Herdr's opencode asset at version 10 does map retry to working, so this is a place where the kilo asset is behind its sibling and the port chose fidelity over improvement.

tool_use is NOT claimed, and the reason is that the branch is unreachable rather than that tool use is uninteresting. tool.execute.before and tool.execute.after are plugin HOOKS in kilo, invoked through Plugin.trigger, and not bus events, so an `event` handler never sees them. traces/kilo/tool-turn.tsv is a turn in which a bash tool really ran, with the command and its output in the run log, and neither name appears anywhere between chat.message and session.idle. Herdr lists both in its event switch in its kilo and its opencode assets alike, so those two branches are dead code against this release. Sidecar keeps them, because they cost one comparison and would be correct if kilo ever published the names, and does not claim the transition on the strength of them.

Cancellation is not distinguishable by this asset, so `cancelled` is unclaimed. A user interrupt reaches the bus as session.error carrying error.name=MessageAbortedError, the same shape a provider failure takes with a different name, and upstream's kilo asset maps every session.error to the blocked lane without reading the name at all. The port keeps that mapping and traces/kilo/error-turn.tsv shows why it is safe rather than merely tolerated: session.status idle arrives one millisecond after the error and closes the lane. What is lost is only the terminal outcome, which is the same conclusion the OpenCode entry reached before its own cancellation traces, and closing it here would mean diverging from upstream's provider half rather than fixing a bug in it.

process_exit is NOT claimed and the asset subscribes to no dispose hook. Kilo does call a plugin's `dispose` on teardown, and Sidecar's OpenCode asset uses exactly that to release the lane, so this is a difference between the two ports rather than a limitation of the provider. Upstream's kilo asset has never had a dispose hook and the provider half is kept verbatim; Sidecar already owns process liveness for every provider, so nothing is lost today. This gap and `covered` move together if a future asset version subscribes.

The unblock evidence is real but was not produced by a human. traces/kilo/blocked-turn.tsv was captured under `kilo run`, which is non-interactive, so the runner answered its own permission prompt one millisecond after asking it. Both events exist, in that order, with the payload fields the asset's branches read, which is what the transition claim rests on. It says nothing about how long a real prompt waits at a TUI.

There are no subagent events and no child-session tracking. Kilo publishes `info.parentID` on its session events, and Herdr's opencode asset at version 10 uses it to keep a child session's events from replacing the pane's root session; the kilo asset has never had that code and the port did not add it, because adding it would be importing a sibling asset's feature rather than fixing a bug. A subagent's session.status therefore drives the pane's lane. All four traces record info.parentID=absent, so nothing here measures the case.

Both plugin/ and plugins/ are loaded. Kilo globs {plugin,plugins}/*.{ts,js} inside every config directory it discovers, so an asset present in both fires every event twice, exactly as on OpenCode. Measured with two probe plugins, one per directory, both of which loaded and ran. The installer owns plugin/ and reports anything with its asset's name in plugins/ as needs-repair.

A non-function export does NOT disqualify a kilo plugin module, which is where kilo is laxer than the OpenCode it forked from. Kilo's loader walks the module namespace and skips an export it cannot call, so a factory beside a string export still runs; measured on 7.5.9 with a probe plugin. OpenCode 1.18.25 drops the whole module in that case, silently. Sidecar's asset holds itself to the stricter convention anyway, because the cost is zero and relying on a fork staying laxer than its upstream is a bet nobody promised to honour.

Kilo also loads ~/.kilo/, ~/.kilocode/, and project-local .kilo/ and .kilocode/ directories walking up from the working directory. Sidecar installs into none of them: a per-project copy would follow a checkout into other people's clones and would report from panes Sidecar never set up.

KILO_CONFIG_DIR relocates kilo's config directory and the installer honours it, as it honours XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Herdr hardcodes ~/.config/kilo and therefore misses both. IT IS NOT ENOUGH TO ISOLATE A PROOF RUN, and that was learned by leaking: kilo still creates its XDG default config directory at startup whatever KILO_CONFIG_DIR says, and the run that proved this integration wrote one zero-byte migration marker into the maintainer's real ~/.config/kilo before the mistake was caught. The file was removed and the directory restored to its previous contents. Anyone tracing a future version must move XDG_CONFIG_HOME as well as KILO_CONFIG_DIR.

The screen lane did not answer for the proof pane, so for kilo the hooks lane was the only lane. `agent explain` reported screenEvidence=unsupported-agent throughout, on a pane whose foreground command tmux reports as `node` because kilo installs as a `#!/usr/bin/env node` shim. The session binding was still accepted, but that is weaker evidence than it looks: CheckReportedKind refuses only a positively identified occupant of a DIFFERENT kind and passes an unidentified one, so exit 0 does not establish that process identity named the pane kilo. What this run measured is that hooks author the lane; what it did not measure is whether the screen fallback can answer for a kilo pane at all.

`agent report-session --kind kilo` was refused until the live proof found it. resolveReportedKind resolved a --kind claim through agentcatalog.Lookup, which searches the launchable families and their aliases only; kilo is detection-only today, so every binding the asset sent failed with exit 5 while its state reports, which take no --kind, were accepted. No offline test could have caught it, because every test in the tree passed a launchable id. The lookup now falls back to the detection catalog, which is the right rule for a verb that answers a question about a pane rather than about a launch.

No event carries a transcript path, so the session binding is by id only. That is enough for identity and for the run fingerprint the store derives, and it is less than a path would give a future resume, which is why no store root is recorded for kilo.

The plugin interface publishes no version or stability guarantee, and kilo is a fast-moving fork of a fast-moving upstream: 7.5.9 was the latest release on the day of capture and the dist-tags carry a separate `next` line at 1.0.8. An integration written against 7.5.9 has no contractual reason to keep working on 7.6, which is why testedProviderRange is the single version actually driven and not a range.
sourceVersionNote: kilo 7.5.9 (@kilocode/cli) on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-09-03 against openrouter z-ai/glm-5.3-flash. The CLI was installed into a scratch npm prefix and run with HOME and every XDG variable pointed at a temporary tree, so the maintainer's real ~/.config/kilo was never read or written; the prefix is removed after the run. The contract was first read from the shipped binary itself (the SessionStatus schema, the {plugin,plugins} glob, the plugin loader's export walk, the KILO_CONFIG_DIR reference embedded in its own configuration guide) and then every load-bearing claim was backed by a capture. Traces are in testdata/traces/kilo. The event mapping is ported from Herdr's kilo integration at HERDR_INTEGRATION_VERSION=4; see internal/agentintegration/portedfrom.go.The integration was then proved live on the same version: Sidecar's own asset was installed by `sidecar agent integration install kilo` rather than by hand, and a kilo TUI in a Sidecar-managed shell on a private tmux server drove `agent report-session --kind kilo --id ...`, then working/turn_start, then idle/turn_complete, all accepted, with `agent explain --shell` reading state=idle authority=lifecycle tier=advisory source=sidecar.kilo.plugin integrationStatus=current and screenState=unknown throughout. Uninstalling and ending the run flipped the lane to authority=screen fallbackReason=process_generation_mismatch.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single SessionStart hook entry: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects. grok has the strongest hook contract in the catalog and this asset asks for none of it.
Not traced. Every statement here is read from the documentation grok 1.0.13 embeds in its own shipped binary, so the tier rests on documentation rather than on a capture.

grok loads hooks from ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.cursor/hooks.json as well as its own ~/.grok/hooks/*.json, so Sidecar's Claude and Cursor entries also fire inside grok sessions, each claiming its own --kind. Exactly one of the three binds: report-session canonicalises the kind through the catalog and then verifies it against the pane's own occupant, so the foreign claims are refused with kind_mismatch. That is td-11040b, and TestBothEntriesFireInAGrokSessionAndOnlyGroksBinds drives the Claude and grok entries against a grok-typed shell.
The reverse direction is safe by construction rather than by a check: Claude does not read ~/.grok/hooks/, so Sidecar's grok entry can only ever fire inside grok.

grok's payload is camelCase (hookEventName, sessionId, cwd, workspaceRoot, promptId), and grok also exports GROK_SESSION_ID into every hook process. Herdr's asset prefers the variable and falls back to the payload; Sidecar reads the payload only, because --hook-stdin is one bounded reader serving every provider and a per-provider environment read would be a second way for one provider to name a session. Nothing has been observed where the two disagree.

Sidecar owns a dedicated file, ~/.grok/hooks/sidecar.json, because grok merges every *.json in that directory. Ownership is still by entry rather than by file: a hook a user adds to that file is preserved, and the file is removed only when Sidecar's entry was all it held. Herdr deletes its equivalent file outright.
GROK_HOME relocates the configuration home and is honoured. Herdr also honours a GROK_CONFIG_DIR, and its own comment says the grok CLI does not read it, so Sidecar does not follow that one.

Hooks are deduplicated across layers by identical handler, and grok's own Stop hook defaults to a 600 second timeout while other events default to 5. Sidecar's entry declares 10 explicitly on SessionStart.

grok's contract would support `full` once traced -- it is the only provider anywhere with a dedicated cancellation event, StopCancelled, carrying user_interrupt, permission_rejected, permission_cancelled, max_turns and no_progress, alongside PermissionDenied, StopFailure and Notification{permission_prompt, idle_prompt}. The ceiling is a target, not a claim.
sourceVersionNote: grok 1.0.13 on darwin/arm64. The hook locations table, the event list, the JSON and TOML hook formats, the camelCase payload fields, GROK_SESSION_ID, and the Claude and Cursor compatibility sources were all read from the documentation the shipped binary embeds, which documents StopCancelled where the vendor website does not. Ported from Herdr's grok integration version 1.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single sessionStart hook entry: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects. Cursor's own contract is far broader.

Not traced. The contract was read out of cursor-agent 2026.08.25's shipped bundle rather than observed, and there are user reports of events being omitted on particular versions, so tracing stays mandatory before any tier above this one.

The hooks file is ~/.cursor/hooks.json and no environment override moves it. cursor-agent HAS a configuration-directory resolver reading CURSOR_CONFIG_DIR then $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cursor then ~/.cursor, but its hook loader does not use it: the user hooks path is built from homedir() and ".cursor" directly in the same bundle. Herdr honours CURSOR_CONFIG_DIR, which would put an entry in a directory the loader never opens, so Sidecar does not.

Event names are camelCase (sessionStart, beforeSubmitPrompt, postToolUseFailure) while the payload's field names are snake_case (session_id, hook_event_name, transcript_path), which is Claude's spelling. Both halves of that crossing are Cursor's, not a transcription error.

The entry is the minimal documented shape, a lone `command` member, which is what Herdr writes. Cursor's own generator emits `{type, command}`, so both forms exist in the wild and the scan accepts a handler with no `type`.

cursor-agent also loads hooks from ~/.claude/settings.json and the project-local Claude settings, so Sidecar's Claude entry fires inside cursor sessions too. It is refused there rather than bound, because report-session verifies the claimed kind against the pane's own occupant.

The `version` member at the top of hooks.json is written only into a file Sidecar creates. 2026.08.25's hook loader never reads it, so adding it to a user's existing file would edit bytes outside Sidecar's entry for no effect. Herdr adds it unconditionally.

Sidecar's asset registers nothing else, so the full registry present in the bundle -- beforeSubmitPrompt, the tool events, stop carrying status "aborted", postToolUseFailure.is_interrupt, subagentStart/Stop and sessionEnd -- is a ceiling rather than a claim. A fuller asset could reach `full` on paper once traced.
sourceVersionNote: cursor-agent 2026.08.25 on darwin/arm64. The hooks file path, the flat handler array, the payload's field names and the absence of any version check were read out of the shipped bundle rather than from documentation. Ported from Herdr's cursor integration version 1.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single SessionStart hook entry: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects.

This is the weakest evidence in the registry, and the reason is stated first rather than buried: GitHub Copilot CLI is not installed on any machine Sidecar has surveyed, so every fact in this entry comes from Herdr's installer and its vendored asset rather than from a released binary. Nothing here has been checked against the provider, including the file path, the entry shape and the field names.

The entry's shape is Herdr's, faithfully, and it is three departures from every other provider in this registry: `type` is `command`, the command lives under `bash` rather than `command`, and the timeout is `timeoutSec` rather than `timeout`.

`bash` is written unconditionally rather than switched to `powershell` on Windows the way Herdr does, because Sidecar does not run on Windows and the Windows spelling would be unreachable and untestable. The scan reads both spellings, so an entry written in the other form is still recognised as Sidecar's and can still be removed.

$COPILOT_HOME is honoured as the configuration-directory override, on Herdr's word alone. If a released Copilot turns out not to read it, honouring it sends an install where nothing reads, and the fix is to drop it the way Antigravity's Herdr-only seam was dropped.

Herdr's installer removes its own registrations from nine other events -- UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, agentStop, SessionEnd, notification and sessionStart -- which is the rollback of a full-lifecycle hook set it used to ship. Sidecar never shipped those, so there is nothing to roll back; the ownership rule finds a Sidecar entry on any event regardless.

Interrupt appears to be reported at session granularity rather than per turn, which would not distinguish a cancelled turn from a closed session. That was the reading before this port and nothing since has tested it.
Not traced, and cannot be traced on this machine. A capture needs a released Copilot CLI and credentials the environment does not carry.

knownGaps: The shipped asset is a single PreInvocation hook entry: session identity only, by design, and that is what the tier reflects.

Antigravity has no session start or end event at all. Its whole hook surface is five events -- PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreInvocation, PostInvocation and Stop -- so there is no moment that means "this session began" and the conversation is named by whichever event fires first. PreInvocation is that event: it fires before the model is called, on every turn, where the tool events fire only for a turn that calls a tool.

There is no blocking event and no cancellation event, so neither the blocked lane nor process exit could be authored from these hooks even if the asset tried. Stop carries a terminationReason and a fullyIdle flag and is the only turn-end signal; PreToolUse can return a decision, but a hook deciding is not the same as a hook being told the user was asked.

The payload is camelCase, because Antigravity encodes it with protojson. The session id arrives as conversationId and the transcript as transcriptPath, neither of which is a field name any other provider in this registry uses.

A hook must write a JSON object to stdout, so Sidecar's entry appends `printf '{}\n'` after the report command, which prints nothing on success. The suffix is also what makes the hook fail open, because the exit status Antigravity sees is printf's.

The hooks configuration path has already moved between releases: agy's own changelog records fixing its /hooks command writing to ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/hooks.json instead of the shared ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json. The installer targets the shared one, which is where 1.1.22 reads.

Antigravity honours no environment override for that directory. Herdr honours ANTIGRAVITY_CLI_CONFIG_DIR, but the variable appears nowhere in the shipped binary, so it is Herdr's test seam rather than the provider's contract and Sidecar does not follow it. Relocating the provider for a test means moving HOME.
Not traced. Every statement here is read from agy 1.1.22's own embedded hooks documentation and from the vendored Herdr asset, so the tier rests on documentation rather than on a capture.
Hooks run synchronously and block the agent loop, and only type "command" is supported. A slow report would slow a turn, which is why the entry declares a ten second timeout.

knownGaps: No Sidecar integration is built, so nothing is claimed and screen detection remains the sole authority.

Muse Spark 1.0.1 traced locally (darwin/arm64, echo provider) but hooks are not shipped: Muse Code's extension surface is skills, MCP servers, and the MSP wire schema, not lifecycle hooks. No published hook contract like Claude Code's hooks or Codex's hooks.json was found in the binary or docs at https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code/.

The session log (JSONL at ~/.local/share/muse/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/<uuid>/session.jsonl) and SQLite index at ~/.local/share/muse/session-index.db are the durable stores; reasoning text is encrypted (encrypted_content) and tool call/result shapes are visible but not hook-authored.
Screen detection is therefore the sole lane authority; the capability entry exists so the provider appears in the matrix and can be promoted when and if Muse ships lifecycle hooks.
sourceVersionNote: muse 1.0.1 on darwin/arm64, inspected 2026-08-31. No hook contract found; session storage verified via local JSONL and SQLite traces, and live TUI captured via private tmux socket (braille title spinner U+2800-FF, ◈ Thinking + esc to interrupt chrome, ⟩ prompt idle).

knownGaps: TRACED, and `advisory` is the ceiling these traces can reach rather than a waypoint. Four sanitized captures of kimi-code 0.40.1 are in testdata/traces/kimi: one TUI turn with a Bash call that needed approval, a turn interrupted with Escape, the SessionEnd that follows /quit, and the same tool call under the non-interactive `kimi -p`. Between them they cover five of the seven transitions FullLifecycleTransitions names, plus tool_use, which the covered list carries but that function does not. The two it does name and this port does not reach are session_identity, which is the gap below, and process_exit, which is unclaimed by choice; `full` needs both.

Session identity cannot be bound on this build, and the cause is in Sidecar rather than in Kimi. Kimi's SessionStart payload carries a session_id -- traces/kimi/tool-turn-with-permission.tsv records it -- and the shipped hook table has a SessionStart row that passes it to `sidecar agent report-session --hook-stdin`. That command canonicalises its --kind through agentcatalog.Lookup, which searches the launchable families and their aliases only; kimi is a detection-only family, so Lookup("kimi") is false. Measured live in the proof run: the command exits 5 with `unsupported_kind: "kimi" is not an agent kind Sidecar knows`. State reports are unaffected, because `agent report` checks --provider against the pane's resolved occupant instead and agentactivity identifies a kimi process by name. The row ships anyway: it is correct and inert rather than wrong, and it starts working the moment kimi becomes a family the catalog resolves, which is Slice 5 of the parity plan. `session_identity` is unclaimed until it does.

Kimi runs every hook matching an event in parallel, so two rows matching one event would be two report processes racing for a store sequence. Upstream's table avoids it by construction -- the only doubled event is PreToolUse and its two matchers are exact complements -- and a row added later without a complementary matcher would reintroduce the race silently. TestKimiFiresExactlyOneHookPerEvent is the guard.

The blocked lane resolves through ONE event, and that is what makes it claimable. PermissionResult fires whether the user approves or denies and carries the outcome in a `decision` field, so upstream's single unblocking row is sufficient. Claude Code caps below full authority because a denial emits nothing at all and the pane latches; Codex escapes that only because denial takes a different event from approval. Kimi needs neither workaround.

The blocked lane is reachable only from an interactive session. Under `kimi -p` the same Bash call runs with no PermissionRequest and no PermissionResult between PreToolUse and PostToolUse -- there is nobody to ask, so it approves -- which is recorded in traces/kimi/exec-turn-auto-approves.tsv and is why the blocked evidence had to come from a real TUI.

The PreToolUse working row uses upstream's negative-lookahead matcher `^(?!AskUserQuestion$).*$`. Kimi loads it: `kimi doctor` reported the config Sidecar wrote as valid, and the live run produced exactly one working report for a Bash PreToolUse. What is NOT proved is the other side of the complement, because no captured turn used the AskUserQuestion tool: whether that matcher excludes it, rather than merely including everything else, is untraced. If the lookahead were ignored, the symptom would be a working report racing the blocked one on a question.

process_exit is NOT claimed and SessionEnd is deliberately not hooked. Upstream's twelve rows do not include it and this port keeps the provider half verbatim. The event is real and readable: traces/kimi/session-end.tsv is a SessionEnd carrying reason=exit, captured by typing /quit. So a future asset that released the lane on that reason could claim the transition; today it is unclaimed by choice, and this gap and `covered` move together when that changes.

cancelled is claimed as a lane and is deliberately not a terminal outcome. Interrupt fires carrying reason=cancelled and upstream maps it to idle, which is what this port sends; no `sidecar agent end --outcome cancelled` accompanies it, because a turn interrupt is not a run ending. StopFailure, which Kimi publishes for a failed turn, is not hooked by upstream and not hooked here, so a provider error resolves through whatever event follows it rather than through a lane of its own -- untraced.

Sub-agent activity is visible only as SubagentStart, which upstream maps to working, and there is no SubagentStop row, so a sub-agent cannot return the pane to idle on its own. The turn's own Stop does that. Whether a sub-agent's PreToolUse events carry a distinguishing field is unknown: no captured turn spawned one. PermissionRequest does carry an agent_id, which suggests they are separable, but that is a field name in a fixture rather than a measurement.

SessionHeartbeat fires roughly every 60 seconds for the life of a session and is not hooked, by upstream or here. It is worth knowing it exists: it is the only event that would let a hooks lane notice a wedged provider on its own, and today that job belongs to the freshness policy and process liveness.

The integration manages one file, $KIMI_CODE_HOME/config.toml or ~/.kimi-code/config.toml. Kimi also reads a project-local .kimi-code/local.toml; Sidecar deliberately does not install there, because a per-project copy would follow a checkout into other people's clones and report from panes Sidecar never set up.

Ownership is by marker comment, so a hook of Sidecar's that a user copies outside the managed block is detected and refused. A hook of theirs that WRAPS the command in a script of their own is not: the ownership rule reads the first word of the command and a wrapper is not the sidecar binary. That fails in the documented direction -- their entry is never adopted or deleted -- but it means such a duplicate reports alongside Sidecar's own and is invisible to `integration status`. Observed during the proof run, where a debug wrapper produced a second idle report for one Stop.

config.toml is edited by a line editor that only ever replaces the region between its own two marker comments, with a TOML parser as a read-only oracle at both ends of every edit. A config.toml containing a structural multi-line string is refused outright -- install, repair and uninstall all decline rather than risk a marker comment inside a string body -- so the integration is unavailable to a user whose config uses one. That fails in the safe direction.
sourceVersionNote: kimi-code 0.40.1 on darwin/arm64, traced 2026-09-03 against openrouter openai/gpt-4.1-mini. The contract was first read from Kimi Code CLI's own published hooks reference (twenty events; a four-field [[hooks]] schema of event, matcher, command and timeout, where any extra field makes the whole config fail to load; a stdin payload carrying hook_event_name, session_id, session_title, client_type and cwd; fail-open exit-code semantics) and its configuration reference ($KIMI_CODE_HOME, ~/.kimi-code/config.toml); every load-bearing claim is now backed by a capture. Kimi 0.40.1 was installed into a scratch prefix with KIMI_INSTALL_DIR and KIMI_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1, its data directory redirected with KIMI_CODE_HOME, and driven in a real TUI inside a Sidecar-managed shell on a private tmux server with XDG_STATE_HOME, -config and SIDECAR_ISOLATED_STATE=1 under a scratch tree; the user's real ~/.kimi-code was never created. Sidecar's own block was installed by `sidecar agent integration install kimi` rather than by hand, so the run proves the installer too, and `kimi doctor` reported the resulting config.toml valid. The hooks lane was proved end to end: the store recorded working(turn_start), working(tool_use), blocked(permission_request), working(permission_resolved), idle(turn_complete) and idle(cancelled) from source sidecar.kimi.hooks with store-assigned sequences 1..8 and no gaps. The event-to-lane mapping is ported row for row from Herdr's kimi integration at HERDR_INTEGRATION_VERSION=7, whose minimum supported Kimi Code is 0.14.0; see internal/agentintegration/portedfrom.go.
